AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Subdural empyema can present as a spinal subdural empyema (SSE) or a cranial subdural empyema (CSE). Though they differ somewhat in epidemiology, etiology, pathophysiology, and symptomatology and occur separately, they rarely manifest together. The aim of this article is to review the literature concerning the clinical presentation, clinical course and treatment options for managing concurrently-occurring SSE and CSE.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: The literature in the Medline database was reviewed with keywords including but not limited to subdural empyema, retroclival empyema, and Streptococcus mitis. No similar reports were found in the database involving infection with this type of microorganism in this anatomical region.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Only three cases with concurrent CSE and SSE were found in the literature caused by various etiological agents. Two of the patients recovered with no neurological deficit while one fatality was reported. One new illustrative case caused by Streptococcus mitis is also presented.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: CSE and SSE are neurosurgical emergencies, often requiring prompt surgical evacuation. Although very rare, Streptococcus mitis can cause spinal subdural empyema or retroclival abscesses. Natural history of this disease is grave without treatment. Delays in diagnosis and treatment are directly related to mortality and severe morbidity in patients with intracranial and spinal subdural empyema. Prompt recognition and treatment are essential to preclude severe neurological disabilities or in rare cases a fatal outcome. A treatment paradigm for cranio-spinal empyema is proposed.
